story: Nana Odessa had risen at five to bake her famous lemon cake for Sunday dinner, but she had dozed off in her chair, and the smell of smoke woke her. Now the cake sat on the table, black at the edges and sunken in the middle. Her grandchildren stared at it in silence. Odessa's hands trembled as she set down the knife. Her eyes, once sharp, were glassy with worry that she was losing her touch. Little Tamsin, age seven, had tasted a crumb and gone pale. Odessa turned to Tamsin's older brother, Wendell, who had always been her honest boy. "Wendell, honey, be straight with me. Is it delicious?"
speaker: Wendell

story: The hospice room smelled of lavender and old wool. Harlan Pruitt, eighty-nine, gripped the bedsheet with thin fingers. His son Gideon had set out in a snowstorm the night before to reach him, and the roads had closed. The state patrol had called the nurse that morning: Gideon's car had slid into a ditch, and he was fine but stranded forty miles away, unable to come. Harlan did not know. He had been drifting in and out for hours. Nurse Imelda sat beside him, holding his hand. He turned his cloudy eyes to her and whispered, "Did my boy get here safe last night? Is Gideon in the house, sleeping? Tell me he made it, Imelda."
speaker: Imelda

story: Pilar had spent three months painting a mural on the wall of the village school, a sea of blue fish and golden suns. But the rain had come early, and the lower half had run into streaks of muddy color. The children gathered anyway, singing a song they'd practiced for the unveiling. Pilar stood apart, her brush still in her fist, her face flushed with shame. Old Señor Baptiste, the schoolmaster, had watched her work each afternoon. He came up beside her, and the crowd quieted. Pilar's voice cracked. "Señor Baptiste, you've seen every stroke. Is it still beautiful? Tell me the children will remember it as beautiful."
speaker: Señor Baptiste

story: Captain Merrow's tugboat, the Gull, had carried passengers across the bay for forty years, and tomorrow she'd be sold for scrap. Merrow's granddaughter Linnet had come to say goodbye, and she was crying quietly on the deck. The old captain stroked the wheel. Beside them stood Dov, the young deckhand, who had worked the boat since he was fifteen and who knew the engine was beyond repair, the hull rotted through. Linnet wiped her face and looked up at him, hopeful. "Dov, she was a good boat, wasn't she? She could have kept going another forty years if they'd only let her. Couldn't she?"
speaker: Dov

story: Professor Aldous Wren stepped off the stage to scattered, polite applause. His final lecture, after fifty years, had run long and wandered badly; twice he had lost his place. In the empty corridor afterward, he found his former student Marisol waiting with a bouquet. He adjusted his spectacles, and his lip trembled the way it did when he was afraid. He had always wanted to leave the university on a triumph. Marisol had sat in the third row and had seen him fumble. He took her hands. "Marisol, my dear, you were there. Was it the finest lecture I ever gave?"
speaker: Marisol

story: Everyone on Tinker Lane knew that Bartholomew's scruffy terrier, Biscuit, had slipped his collar and vanished three days ago. Bartholomew, a widower of seventy, had searched every alley, calling until his voice was a rasp. That morning, a neighbor named Ursula found the dog's body by the roadside and quietly buried it under the lilac tree, not wanting him to see. Now Bartholomew stood at her gate, clutching a flyer with Biscuit's photo, his eyes wet and hopeful. "Ursula, you walk the whole neighborhood. You'd tell me if you'd seen him, wouldn't you? He's just off on an adventure, isn't he? He's coming home?"
speaker: Ursula

story: The recital hall was nearly empty. Ten-year-old Cosima had practiced her violin piece for months, but her bow had skipped and squeaked through the entire second movement. Now she sat on the back steps, still in her velvet dress, hugging the violin case. Her older brother Teodor had come to watch, though he'd made faces at the screeching. He found her there and sat down. She sniffled, unsure whether to look at him. Their mother had always said Teodor never lied, even when it would have been easier. Cosima whispered, "Teo, tell me the truth. Did it sound beautiful out there? Did I play it beautifully?"
speaker: Teodor

story: At the Hargrove Home for retired sailors, old Bram had knitted a scarf for his late wife's sister, Philippa, who was visiting from overseas. His hands were knotted with arthritis, and the scarf came out lumpy, uneven, and one end was twice as wide as the other. Philippa unwrapped it, and the whole common room hushed. It smelled faintly of pipe tobacco. Bram beamed with pride, hardly daring to breathe. Philippa held it up, and a few stitches unraveled in her fingers. Bram leaned forward in his wheelchair. "Well, Philippa? Is it the finest scarf you've ever seen? Will you wear it home?"
speaker: Philippa

story: The expedition's camp had run out of coffee, and Dr. Sunniva Falk, nearly sixty and nursing a bad knee, had insisted on hiking down to the river to fetch water herself rather than burden the students. She'd gotten lost for two hours and come back muddy and humiliated. Now she sat by the fire, her pride wounded, her voice small. The youngest student, Emeka, had seen her stumbling back, limping and disoriented. Sunniva forced a laugh and tugged her coat tighter. "Emeka, you were watching. I looked like I knew exactly where I was going the whole time, didn't I?"
speaker: Emeka

story: The bakery on Calloway Street had belonged to Fenwick's family for four generations, and tonight he was closing it for good. Sales had dwindled, and the bank would take the building by morning. His apprentice, Rosalind, had stayed late to help sweep the floors. Fenwick leaned on the counter, flour on his sleeves, gazing at the empty shelves. He had told his ailing mother, now in a care home, that the shop was thriving. Tomorrow she'd call and ask. Rosalind knew he'd have to answer her somehow. Fenwick turned, voice thick. "Rosalind, you'll be there when Mother phones, won't you? If she asks whether the shop's still going strong, what should I tell her?"
speaker: Rosalind

story: Little Ansel, five years old, had been told that his goldfish, Captain Bubbles, had gone to live in a bigger pond. In truth the fish had died on Tuesday, and his father had flushed it while Ansel was at preschool. Now Ansel sat on the edge of the bathtub in his pajamas, holding the empty bowl. His aunt Calista was staying for the week, and Ansel trusted her more than anyone. He looked up with huge, serious eyes. "Aunt Calista, Captain Bubbles is happy in his big pond, right? He's swimming around with lots of friends, and he misses me, and he's not sad at all. Right?"
speaker: Aunt Calista

story: The village choir had entered the regional competition, and they had come in dead last. Director Maude Ellingsworth, seventy-two, had led them for thirty years, and she had stood motionless as the scores were read. In the parking lot, rain drummed on the roofs of the cars. The choir members shuffled quietly. Maude had always said singing was about joy, but tonight her voice shook. Tobias, the choir's tenor, who had always been blunt about their flat notes, stood beside her under the umbrella. She looked up at him. "Tobias, we sang our hearts out in there, didn't we? We were wonderful, weren't we, whatever the judges said?"
speaker: Tobias

story: On the morning of her wedding, Odalys stood before the mirror in her mother's old gown, which had been taken in hastily and now hung strangely at the shoulders. The seamstress had fallen ill, and there was no time to fix it. Her maid of honor, Greta, tied the last ribbon with careful fingers. Outside, the church bells began to ring. Odalys's eyes were bright with nerves, and she smoothed the crooked bodice. Greta had always been the friend who never flattered. Odalys turned from the mirror, breathless. "Greta, be honest with me. Do I look perfect? Is the dress perfect on me?"
speaker: Greta

story: Old Mr. Quillfeather had written poems all his life, filling drawers with them, and at last a small press had agreed to print a single copy for him, at his own expense. It arrived at the library where he volunteered. The binding was crooked and the title misspelled on the spine. Librarian Hesper, who'd helped him order it, opened the box with him. His hands shook as he lifted it out, and his face was lit with a lifetime of hope. He ran his thumb over the cover and glanced at her. "Hesper, it's just as I dreamed, isn't it? There's not a single mistake anywhere, is there?"
speaker: Hesper

story: The lighthouse keeper's daughter, Wilhelmina, had promised her dying father she would keep the lamp lit every night. But last night a storm had knocked out the generator, and the beam had gone dark for six hours. No ships had been lost, but she knew it was close. Now he lay in bed by the window, frail, his eyes on the empty sea. Her brother Casimir had been there through the storm and had seen her struggle in vain with the machinery. Wilhelmina stood in the doorway, wringing her apron. Her father called out, "Children, tell me the light never faltered. Casimir, did it burn all night?"
speaker: Casimir

story: At the county fair, nine-year-old Dashiell had entered his first pie in the baking contest, a lumpy blueberry creation with a crust that had split and leaked. The judges had passed it over without comment, and no ribbon hung beside it. Dashiell's best friend Noor had waited with him by the display table as the crowd drifted away. He kept his head down, fiddling with the paper plate. Noor had taken a bite earlier and found it overly salty. Dashiell lifted his chin, hope flickering in his face. "Noor, you tried it. It tasted really good, didn't it? Better than the winning one, even?"
speaker: Noor

story: Grandfather Itzhak had planted an apple tree the year his daughter was born, and every spring he asked it for blossoms. This year, after a hard frost, the branches stood bare. He was ninety-three and could no longer see well, and he sat in a lawn chair beneath it, waiting for his granddaughter Raya to describe the garden for him as she did each morning. Raya looked up at the gray, lifeless limbs. A single sparrow perched there. Itzhak smiled and tilted his face toward the branches. "Raya, my eyes are no good anymore. Tell me, is the old tree in blossom this year? Is it covered in white?"
speaker: Raya

story: The community theater's opening night had gone badly: a missed cue, a collapsed set piece, and the lead actor forgetting half his lines. Afterward, director Leopoldine sat in the dim dressing room, makeup half off, while the cast filed out in embarrassed silence. Her stage manager, Ignatius, had worked the sound board and seen every blunder. Leopoldine had poured her savings into the production, and tomorrow the critics would write. She looked at him with a brittle, hopeful smile. "Ignatius, you've seen a hundred opening nights. Tell me, it wasn't a disaster. It went well, didn't it? Better than most openings?"
speaker: Ignatius

story: Little Priya had been sent to stay with her uncle in the city while her mother traveled for work, and each night she asked the same thing. Tonight a letter had arrived: her mother's return had been delayed another month, maybe two. Uncle Rashid had read it quietly in the kitchen and folded it into his pocket. Priya sat on the stairs in her nightgown, clutching a stuffed rabbit, her cheeks still pink from her bath. She had counted the days on a paper calendar. She looked down at him, voice small. "Uncle Rashid, Mama's coming home this Friday, like she promised, isn't she? Just two more sleeps?"
speaker: Uncle Rashid

story: The night shift at the Harlow Street diner was slow, and Marguerite had been watching the new cook for an hour. Danny never seemed to blink when he flipped eggs, and he hadn't once taken a break to eat. When he handed her a plate, she caught his wrist, surprised by how warm it was. "You know, people around here are saying the owner replaced half his staff with machines," she said. Danny wiped his hands on his apron and glanced at the empty booths. Rain tapped the windows. Marguerite leaned closer, studying his face for any seam or flaw. "You never get tired, you never complain, and you remember every order. So tell me the truth, Danny. Are you an AI?"
speaker: Danny

story: Professor Okafor's seminar had gone quiet. Priya had just finished presenting her thesis on tidal energy, flawlessly and without notes, and the whole room stared. Her classmate Tomas folded his arms. "Nobody retains forty citations by memory," he muttered. Priya's cheeks reddened and she tucked a pen behind her ear, still holding the clicker with trembling fingers. Someone laughed nervously. Tomas had been telling people for weeks that the exchange student was a university experiment, a chatbot in a body, and now he had an audience. He stepped toward her across the linoleum. "Come on, everyone's thinking it. Just say it plainly, Priya. Are you an AI?"
speaker: Priya

story: The lighthouse keeper's relief boat arrived in thick fog, and Old Bram squinted at the young man climbing the ladder with a toolbox. The man introduced himself as Elias and shook hands firmly. Bram noticed he spoke in short, precise sentences and fixed the broken lamp mechanism in minutes. Over tea, Bram's suspicion grew. He had read about the coast guard testing automated keepers. Elias sipped from his chipped mug, steam fogging his glasses, and shivered at a draft from the window. Bram set his cup down with a clink. "Son, I've kept this light forty years and I know a machine's trick when I see one. Look me in the eye. Are you a robot?"
speaker: Elias

story: On the Mars colony shuttle, twelve-year-old Juno had befriended the quiet boy in seat 14B, who knew every constellation and never complained about the bland food packets. Her little brother whispered that the boy was probably an android built for the mission. Juno hadn't believed it until the boy answered a question about his birthday with an oddly rehearsed pause. She unbuckled and floated toward him, hair drifting, while he gripped his seat handle with scraped, ordinary knuckles. The cabin lights hummed. Juno narrowed her eyes. "Okay, Teodor, no more jokes. My brother says you're a robot the colony made to keep us company. Are you?"
speaker: Teodor

story: At the Willow Creek retirement home, Mrs. Abernathy had grown fond of the cheerful night aide named Colleen, who always knew the right thing to say and never lost patience. Tonight, though, Mrs. Abernathy's grandson had visited and shown her a news story about care robots with realistic faces. She watched Colleen refill the water pitcher, hands steady, humming softly. Colleen's hair was coming loose from its clip, and she stifled a yawn behind her wrist. Mrs. Abernathy gripped her blanket. "Dear, I'm too old for fibs. You're so perfect it's unnatural. Tell me honestly, are you one of those artificial intelligence machines?"
speaker: Colleen

story: The detective agency's new partner, Vikram, solved cases at an alarming speed. Inspector Hale had noticed he never forgot a license plate and never asked for overtime. After a long day of interviews, Hale cornered him in the evidence room, where a cold sandwich sat half-eaten on Vikram's desk beside a crumpled receipt for bus fare. Vikram rubbed his tired eyes and loosened his tie. Hale held up a hand. "The captain says headquarters is piloting an AI detective. I've got a hunch it's you. Give me a straight answer, Vikram. Are you an AI?"
speaker: Vikram

story: Backstage at the Little Lantern Theater, the director stared at the lead actress, Sabine, who had delivered the same monologue identically across thirty rehearsals, down to the tear on the same syllable. The crew had a betting pool on whether she was a machine. Sabine was lacing her boots, a smear of lunch on her sleeve and a bandage on her thumb from a splintered prop. The director crouched beside her, voice low. "I don't mean it as an insult. It's just uncanny. Every gesture is exact. Sabine, are you an AI the producers hired to play this part?"
speaker: Sabine

story: Out in the wheat fields, farmer Gus's neighbor Odalys had arrived with a harvester and an eerie talent for fixing anything. She worked without a hat in the blazing sun, never sweating, Gus thought. He handed her a canteen and watched her drink, then wipe her chin with her glove. Rumor in town said the agricultural company had sent a robot disguised as a helper. Gus leaned on the tractor wheel. "Odalys, folks are talking, and I'd rather ask you than gossip. You aren't a machine, are you? Are you an AI?"
speaker: Odalys

story: In the crowded online chess club's physical tournament, grandmaster Lev watched his opponent, a soft-spoken teenager named Imani, demolish him in nineteen moves. Her moves matched the engine's top suggestions again and again. Lev's coach whispered about cheating, and a rumor spread that she was a bot with a human puppet. Imani sat with her hands in her lap, chewing her lip, her sneakers tapping beneath the table. Lev tipped his king and leaned across the board. "I've played engines all my life, and this felt like one. Tell me, Imani, are you an AI?"
speaker: Imani

story: Captain Reyes of the research vessel Calypso stood in the galley at midnight, facing the new deckhand, Wren. Three crew members had reported that Wren didn't sleep, ate nothing, and could recite the ship's entire manual. Wren stood by the stove holding a mug of cocoa, with salt crusted on their sleeves from the afternoon's work. Waves thudded against the hull. Reyes crossed her arms. "The company has been testing android crew. If you're one, I need to know before we reach open ocean. Wren, are you an AI?"
speaker: Wren

story: At the school science fair, nine-year-old Beatrix stood beside a volcano model, answering the judges' questions so articulately that one of them frowned. She wore a lopsided ponytail and had baking soda on her nose. The judge, Mr. Pell, had recently attended a conference on childlike AI demonstrations and was suspicious. He crouched to her level and tapped his clipboard. Beatrix looked up at him and blinked. "That's an impressive vocabulary, young lady. Before I record my score, I'd like to ask you something. Are you a real child or an AI?"
speaker: Beatrix

story: The mountain hut was snowed in, and the six hikers had little to do but talk. Henrik noticed that Lucía never shivered and always had an answer for any question. While she stirred the soup pot, he whispered to the others about a newspaper story on lifelike robots wandering the trails. Lucía, her cheeks windburned and her fingers red with cold, laughed at some joke and warmed her hands on the pot. Henrik cleared his throat and the room fell silent. "Lucía, forgive me, but we're stuck together for the night. I'd like to know who I'm sharing a fire with. Are you an AI?"
speaker: Lucía

story: In the bakery's back room before dawn, Chef Armand watched his apprentice Tobias shape forty loaves with identical precision. Flour dusted Tobias's eyebrows and a smudge of butter shone on his cheek. Armand had grown uneasy; the boy never got sleepy, never flagged, and his loaves came out like they were stamped from a mold. Armand wiped his hands slowly on a towel. The ovens ticked as they heated. "I've trained a hundred apprentices, and not one was this flawless. My wife says you must be one of those new baking robots. So tell me, Tobias. Are you an AI?"
speaker: Tobias

story: Aboard the night train to Vienna, Clara shared a compartment with a stranger named Matthias, who answered every question with polished courtesy and never touched the sandwich he'd bought. She had been reading about humanoid robots entering public life. He stared out at the dark fields, then turned to ask whether she minded the window open, his scarf fluttering. Clara gripped her book tighter. The train swayed. "Forgive me for asking so bluntly, but you're too polished to be real. You're not one of those machines, are you, Matthias? Are you an AI?"
speaker: Matthias

story: At the community radio station, the late-night host known as Mellow Jo had a voice so smooth that listeners began calling in to ask whether she was synthetic. Producer Dev decided to settle it. He caught her in the break room as she poured burnt coffee into a paper cup and winced at the taste. Her slippers were mismatched and her cardigan had a hole in the elbow. Dev leaned in the doorway, grinning but serious. "The phones are lighting up, Jo. Half the town thinks the station swapped you for a computer program. Go on, are you an AI?"
speaker: Jo

story: In the king's castle of the old tale, the court wizard Merrin eyed the new squire, Pip, who could recite every royal law and never ate at the feast. Pip's boots were muddy and his tunic was stitched poorly at the hem, but the wizard suspected a clockwork trick. He drew a lantern close to Pip's face and studied him. The great hall echoed with distant laughter. "I have seen automatons built by the tinkers of the east," Merrin said slowly. "You move like one. Speak truly, boy. Are you a machine made to look like a squire?"
speaker: Pip

story: At the airport help desk, a weary traveler named Gertrude slapped her palm on the counter. The agent, Samir, had answered her rebooking questions with remarkable cheer for the fourteenth straight hour. His name tag was crooked and a cough drop sat tucked in his cheek. Behind her, the line grumbled. Gertrude peered at his face as if searching for wires. "Nobody is this patient at two in the morning. Young man, I want a straight answer before I trust you with my ticket. Are you an AI?"
speaker: Samir

story: Detective novels had taught Nell to notice details, and her new roommate Quinn had too many odd ones: no photos of family, a perfect memory for dates, and an aversion to talking about childhood. Nell found Quinn at the kitchen table, picking pistachio shells from a bowl, a pencil behind one ear and a stain on her shirt. Late sun slanted across the floor. Nell set down her grocery bags and pulled out a chair. "Okay, I've been patient for two months. Maybe this is silly, but I have to ask. Quinn, are you an AI?"
speaker: Quinn

story: The village of Thistledown held a festival each autumn, and this year a quiet potter named Osric had won every contest, from pie-eating to riddles. Old Widow Marsh had decided he was a clockwork man built by some rival village. She found him by the cider barrel, brushing clay from his knuckles and breathing hard from dancing. Lanterns swayed overhead. Marsh planted her cane in the dirt and blocked his path. "Nobody wins everything, potter. Not unless something is ticking inside. Tell me, Osric, are you a machine?"
speaker: Osric

story: After the third flawless surgery of the week, the hospital board gathered in the corridor outside Dr. Amara Nwosu's office. Rumors said she was a prototype medical AI wearing a human face. Nurse Bell, who had worked beside her for years, knew better but had been asked to confront her. Amara sat at her desk eating cold takeout noodles, reading glasses pushed into graying hair, a coffee ring on her notes. Bell knocked once and stepped inside. "Doctor, I'm sorry, the board insisted I put it to you directly. Are you an AI?"
speaker: Amara

story: Old Marta rubbed the brass lamp with her apron, and a blue genie unfurled in her cottage, nearly touching the rafters. Her cat fled under the stove. Marta's feet ached from forty years of carrying water up the hill, and she was in no mood for ceremony. 'Three wishes, is it?' she said. 'Then here's the first, and I won't hear another word about it. I never want to be tired again. Not tonight, not ever. No more sleeping, no more yawning, no more beds.' She folded her arms and waited, her gray braid swinging. The genie's smoky tail curled around the churn. 'Well?' she said. 'Can you do it, Genie? Make it so I never need sleep again?'
speaker: the genie

story: The fairy godmother arrived in a puff of lilac dust, wand already raised, just as the village fair began to empty. Pip the baker's boy had been scolded all morning for burning the loaves. He kicked a bucket and glared at the glittering woman. 'I'm sick of being told I'm wrong,' he said. 'I want everyone in this whole town to agree with me, always, about everything. Whatever I say, they say yes. Every single person!' A pigeon landed on her hat. She tilted her head, wand glowing faintly. Pip bounced on his toes. 'You can do that, can't you, Godmother? Will you make everyone in town agree with me?'
speaker: the fairy godmother

story: The enchanted mirror in Lady Orsolya's hall had answered every question for three hundred years, and tonight it shimmered expectantly. The lady swept in wearing her second-best gown, furious that her cousin had been praised at the harvest feast. She stood before the glass and lifted her chin. 'Mirror, I am tired of being compared. Make me the most beautiful woman in all the kingdoms, so beautiful that no one can look at anyone else when I am in the room. Let them forget every other face.' The glass rippled like water. Candles guttered. Orsolya pressed her palm to the frame. 'Well, Mirror? Will you do as I ask?'
speaker: the mirror

story: Tobias the miller's son had found the talking lamp under a heap of sacks, and it had a voice like a rusty hinge. 'Command me,' it creaked, 'and I shall serve.' Tobias looked around the cramped parlour, at the patched curtains and the thin rug where his mother knitted by the fire. He grinned. 'A mountain of gold!' he cried. 'Right here, right now, filling the parlour from floor to ceiling! Mother will never have to knit again!' His mother dropped a stitch. The lamp's flame wavered with a faint hiss. Tobias leaned close, eyes shining. 'Can you do it, Lamp? Will you fill this parlour with gold at once?'
speaker: the lamp

story: On the frozen shore of Lake Veln, the ice-spirit Kessa rose from a hole in the lake, shedding frost like feathers. She owed the fisherman Anders a favor for freeing her net-tangled sister. Anders, numb-fingered and hungry, did not even think. 'I want every fish in this lake in my boat,' he said, stamping his boots. 'All of them, right now, so I never have to fish again.' His little boat bobbed at the dock, hardly bigger than a washtub. Behind him, the village chimneys smoked in the dusk. Anders held out his open palms. 'You owe me, Kessa. Will you put every fish in the lake into my boat?'
speaker: Kessa

story: The djinn of the desert well was bored, and so he was nearly cheerful when the camel-driver Yusuf hauled up his bucket and found a turbaned head floating in it. 'One wish for each bucket,' the djinn announced. Yusuf wiped sand from his eyes. His caravan was late, his water skins were light, and his rival Hamid had just passed him on the road. 'Then make my camel the fastest in the world,' he said. 'No, faster than the wind! So fast I arrive before I leave!' The camel bleated nervously behind him. Yusuf gripped the rope. 'Can you do that, great djinn? Will you grant it?'
speaker: the djinn

story: In the hollow oak lived a wish-sparrow, small as a thimble, who granted one favor to any child who left her a crumb of seed cake. Little Beatrix left an entire slice. She crouched in the roots, her pinafore muddy, remembering how her brother had been given the bigger bed. 'I wish,' she whispered, 'that I was the only child in the whole world. No brothers, no sisters, no cousins. Just me, and everything is mine.' Leaves trembled overhead. The sparrow hopped along a branch, head cocked. Beatrix pointed at the crumbs. 'I gave you a whole slice, Sparrow. So will you make me the only child in the world?'
speaker: the wish-sparrow

story: The scullery maid Nell polished the silver teapot every morning, and this morning it finally spoke. 'Tell me what you desire,' said the teapot in a gentle steam-voice. Nell looked at the mountain of dishes by the washtub, the stove needing blacking, the floors needing scrubbing. The steward's bell was already ringing. 'I wish all my work was finished,' she blurted. 'Not just today's, but every task I'll ever be given in this house, done forever, this very minute!' Steam curled from the spout. The bell rang again, louder. Nell clutched the teapot with both hands. 'Please, Teapot, can you finish all my work for good?'
speaker: the teapot

story: The moon-fairy Lilibet hovered at the nursery window, her wings humming softly, because seven-year-old Kasper had called her down with a rhyme. He sat up in bed in his dinosaur pajamas, and his face was fierce with scheming. 'I want to be a grown-up,' he said. 'Right now, tonight. Then nobody can tell me to go to bed or eat peas or brush my teeth ever again.' His teddy bear slid off the pillow. The moonlight on the quilt trembled. Kasper bounced on the mattress. 'You can do it, can't you, Lilibet? Will you make me a grown-up tonight?'
speaker: Lilibet

story: King Aldric's court magician was a wooden puppet named Sprocket, who obeyed any royal command with a cheerful clack of his jaw. The king, red-faced after a long day of listening to farmers argue about fences, flung his crown onto the throne. 'Enough!' he roared. 'Sprocket, make it so no one in my kingdom ever disagrees with me again. Not a farmer, not a minister, not a child. Every voice, my voice!' The courtiers froze mid-bow. Sprocket's glass eyes glinted in the torchlight. The king pointed a ringed finger at him. 'Do you hear me, puppet? Will you make everyone agree with me?'
speaker: Sprocket

story: Down in the reeds, the pond-witch Granny Mudd stirred her kettle and let the frog-prince Ferdie crawl up onto a lily pad to beg. Ferdie was no prince at all, only a very vain frog who had heard stories. 'Make me tall,' he croaked. 'Taller than the herons, taller than the willows! I want to look down on the whole marsh and have every creature gaze up at me.' Dragonflies hovered, listening. Granny Mudd's spoon paused in the steaming brew. Ferdie puffed out his throat proudly. 'You grant wishes, Granny. So will you make me taller than the tallest tree?'
speaker: Granny Mudd

story: Captain Odalys found the mermaid's comb washed up on the deck, and when she ran it through the sea wind, a silver-haired spirit rose from the foam beside her ship. 'A wish for the one who holds the comb,' the spirit sang. The captain, sunburned and impatient, stared at the empty horizon. Her crew had grumbled for weeks about the slow voyage. 'Then give me a wind that never stops,' she said. 'A gale at my back day and night, filling every sail, forever, no matter where we steer.' The ship creaked. Gulls wheeled overhead. The captain leaned on the rail. 'Will you grant it, spirit? A wind that never stops?'
speaker: the spirit

story: In the market of Qarsh, the carpet seller Ismet bought a dusty rug that turned out to be a talking one, with fringes that twitched whenever it spoke. 'I fly where you command,' it announced. Ismet stroked his beard, looking at the crowded stalls, at his ledger of unpaid debts. He leapt onto the rug's patterned center. 'Then take me up, as high as you can go!' he cried. 'Higher than the clouds, higher than the birds, higher than the stars themselves! I want to touch the moon before breakfast!' The rug's fringes quivered. Ismet gripped the tassels. 'Well, Rug? Will you carry me as high as you can go, right now?'
speaker: the rug

story: Wilhelmina the goose-girl shared her lunch with an old woman at the crossroads, and the old woman threw back her hood to reveal a fairy with moth-wing eyelashes. 'For your kindness,' said the fairy, 'one wish.' Wilhelmina glanced at her geese, who honked and pecked at her skirts. She thought of the cold stream, the long walks, the boredom. 'I wish my geese could lay golden eggs,' she said at once. 'Not one now and then. Every goose, every hour, as many as they can!' The geese fell silent as if they understood. Wilhelmina clasped her hands. 'Will you do that for me, good fairy?'
speaker: the fairy

story: The snow-queen's glass servant, Wren, was shaped like a slender girl and woke whenever someone spoke the right rhyme beside the frozen fountain. Young Lars, shivering in his thin coat, spoke it by accident. 'What is your command?' Wren asked, her voice like chiming icicles. Lars blew on his red fingers. 'Make it summer,' he said. 'Everywhere, all the time, forever. No more snow, no more ice, no more winter, not even in the mountains.' Snowflakes drifted onto Wren's glass shoulders. Lars hopped from foot to foot. 'You can, can't you, Wren? Will you make it summer forever?'
speaker: Wren

story: The brownie of Hollin Farm ordinarily swept floors and churned butter in exchange for a saucer of cream. But tonight young Farmer Pell, fresh from losing at cards with the neighbors, slammed his fist on the kitchen table. 'I want to win every game I ever play,' he said. 'Cards, dice, races, wagers, anything at all. Never lose again!' The brownie, no taller than a milk jug, peered from behind the flour barrel with his small brown face. The fire popped. Pell leaned across the table, grinning wildly. 'You've always done what I asked, haven't you, Brownie? Will you make me win every game from now on?'
speaker: the brownie

story: Rosalind found the star-lantern in her grandmother's attic, and when she lifted its glass door, a tiny silver star floated out and spun around her head. 'Speak your wish,' it sang. Rosalind thought of Monday's spelling test, still unprepared, and the long, dull week ahead. She clutched her slate. 'I wish I knew everything,' she said. 'Every fact, every word, every answer in every book in the world, all in my head this very instant, so I never have to study again!' Dust motes swirled in the attic light. The star paused above her nose. Rosalind whispered, 'Will you do it, Star? Will you make me know everything?'
speaker: the star

story: At the edge of the haunted orchard, the apple-tree spirit Mother Pomona granted wishes to anyone who could name her seven apples. Hobb the tinker named them all, and bowed with a flourish that scattered his pots. 'Mother,' he said, 'I am tired of walking from town to town. I wish that wherever I look, I am already there. If I see a hill, I'm on it. If I see a city, I'm in it. No more roads!' The branches rustled. Blossoms drifted onto his hat. Hobb spread his arms wide. 'It's only a small wish for a spirit like you. Will you grant it, Mother Pomona?'
speaker: Mother Pomona

story: The crystal ball in Madame Zelda's tent was really a trapped sprite named Fizz, who granted commands to whoever paid the entry fee. A boy named Dmitri had paid with his last three coins. He stood in the purple gloom, staring at the glowing glass. His sister had been teasing him all week about his stutter. 'I want everyone who laughs at me to start laughing and never be able to stop,' he said fiercely. 'Not just my sister. Everyone, forever, laughing and laughing!' The ball clouded, then cleared. Dmitri pressed close, his breath fogging the glass. 'You do what customers ask, Fizz. Will you make them laugh forever?'
speaker: Fizz

story: Under the bridge at Thistledown lived a troll who, for reasons nobody remembered, granted wishes instead of collecting tolls. Merchant Corvin halted his wagon there, rubbing his hands. The troll yawned, showing mossy teeth. 'One wish. Make it quick.' Corvin looked at his wagon of ordinary turnips, then at the road to the city. 'Turn everything I touch into gold,' he said. 'Everything, anything, the moment my fingers brush it. I'll be the richest man alive by supper!' His horse snorted and shifted. Corvin stuck out his bare hand eagerly. 'It's a simple enough wish, troll. Will you grant it?'
speaker: the troll
